conclusion: The incidence/prevalence text difference is real, but a concrete missing testing result is not established after reading the binding parent duties and exact legislative mapping. Withdraw conservatively; retain the discrepancy internally. This is not a declaration of complete transposition or safe practice.
reasoning: Binding parent Article 3(1) requires current medical knowledge. Articles 29(1)(1)–(2) and 30(1)(2)–(3) impose medical justification, necessary examinations and donor/recipient/child risk safeguards as cumulative conditions. Regulation section 2(1)(5) requires other necessary tests and section 3 risk assessment. The incidence rows do not expressly permit withholding another necessary test.

The original government transposition table reproduces corrected prevalence in EU Annex III 2.4 and 3.3 and maps the donor-selection/testing blocks to these statutory duties. Its same legislative package includes draft annex rows saying incidence. This is positive contemporaneous evidence of an intended binding prevalence route, beyond an unrelated generic health provision.

No primary interpretation, official clinical instruction or reasoned legal example was established showing that Polish law permits a test omission in an EU prevalence category after applying those mandatory duties. An actual patient case is unnecessary: concrete legal or authoritative clinical demonstration would suffice.
strongestRetentionCounterargument: The EU rule is categorical. A high-prevalence/low-or-unknown-incidence donor might fall outside a literal table row; individual clinical necessity is not automatically identical to the categorical rule. Explanatory mapping does not amend the regulation or prove current compliance. Preserve this credible research question, without claiming it disproved.
conservativeDecision: Once the specific binding parent route and its express prevalence mapping are considered, the entry does not identify an uncovered legally operative category. Research-only is preferable under the requested threshold. Absence of patient harm is not the reason.
